concepts.title: Final Goods, Intermediate Goods and Double Counting

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Final Goods, Intermediate Goods and Double Counting' refers to.
questions.a: A good bought for end use and not re-entering any production process is final, while one bought as an input and used up in making another good is intermediate; adding both while totaling output would count the same value twice.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Final Goods, Intermediate Goods and Double Counting'.
questions.a: The use of a good, not its physical nature, decides whether it is final or intermediate; counting inputs twice inflates output.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Final Goods, Intermediate Goods and Double Counting', in plain ASCII form.

concepts.title: Consumption Goods, Capital Goods and Consumer Durables

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Consumption Goods, Capital Goods and Consumer Durables' refers to.
questions.a: Final goods split into items consumed on purchase, such as food, and durable items such as machines that aid production for years; long-lived household items like cars or televisions share durability with machines yet still serve consumption.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Consumption Goods, Capital Goods and Consumer Durables'.
questions.a: Durability alone does not make a good capital; its role in production does.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Consumption Goods, Capital Goods and Consumer Durables', in plain ASCII form.

concepts.title: Depreciation, Gross Investment and Net Investment

questions.q: Work out the annual depreciation of a machine from its cost and working life. Use the method 'Depreciation, Gross Investment and Net Investment'. Work with: cost_of_capital_good = 120000, gross_investment = 25, useful_life_years = 150. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of net_investment.

Find the addition to capital stock after allowing for wear and tear. Use the method 'Depreciation, Gross Investment and Net Investment'. Work with: cost_of_capital_good = 5000, gross_investment = 60, useful_life_years = 50. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of net_investment.
Explain in your own words what 'Depreciation, Gross Investment and Net Investment' refers to.
questions.a: Capital wears out as it is used, and the value consumed in a year is depreciation, found by spreading the asset's cost over its expected life; what remains of a year's capital-goods output after replacing worn-out capital is the true addition to the capital stock.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Depreciation, Gross Investment and Net Investment'.
questions.a: Gross investment includes replacement of worn-out capital; only the balance raises the capital stock.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Depreciation, Gross Investment and Net Investment', in plain ASCII form.

concepts.title: Circular Flow of Income and Equivalence of the Three Methods

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Circular Flow of Income and Equivalence of the Three Methods' refers to.
questions.a: In a two-sector economy firms pay households for factor services and households spend those payments back on the firms' products, so the same aggregate can be read as spending, as output value or as factor income, making the product, expenditure and income methods agree.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Circular Flow of Income and Equivalence of the Three Methods'.
questions.a: One circular flow means GDP measured at any of three points must give the same figure.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Circular Flow of Income and Equivalence of the Three Methods', in plain ASCII form.

concepts.title: Value Added or Product Method of Measuring GDP

questions.q: Calculate GDP by the value added method for a chain of firms. Use the method 'Value Added or Product Method of Measuring GDP'. Work with: intermediates_firm1 = 60, intermediates_firm2 = 200, output_firm1 = 150, output_firm2 = 150. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of gdp_product_method.

Find the net contribution of a firm that buys raw material worth 50 and sells output worth 200. Use the method 'Value Added or Product Method of Measuring GDP'. Work with: intermediates_firm1 = 6, intermediates_firm2 = 40, output_firm1 = 25, output_firm2 = 360. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of gdp_product_method.
Explain in your own words what 'Value Added or Product Method of Measuring GDP' refers to.
questions.a: Each firm's contribution equals the value of its output less the value of inputs bought from other firms, and GDP is the sum of these net contributions across every producing firm in the economy.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Value Added or Product Method of Measuring GDP'.
questions.a: Deducting intermediate consumption per firm removes double counting, and summing value added gives GDP.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Value Added or Product Method of Measuring GDP', in plain ASCII form.

concepts.title: Inventories: Stock, Flow and Planned versus Unplanned Change

questions.q: Using the method 'Inventories: Stock, Flow and Planned versus Unplanned Change', work with: opening_inventory = 240, production_during_year = 1500, sales_during_year = 25. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of closing_inventory.

Take the relation taught for 'Inventories: Stock, Flow and Planned versus Unplanned Change' and work with: opening_inventory = 15, production_during_year = 1000, sales_during_year = 25. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of closing_inventory.
Explain in your own words what 'Inventories: Stock, Flow and Planned versus Unplanned Change' refers to.
questions.a: Unsold finished goods, work in progress and raw materials held by a firm form its inventory, a stock measured at a point of time, while the difference between a year's production and sales is the change in inventories, a flow that may be intended or a surprise.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Inventories: Stock, Flow and Planned versus Unplanned Change'.
questions.a: Inventory level is a stock; its change is a flow, and only deviations from the intended change are unplanned.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Inventories: Stock, Flow and Planned versus Unplanned Change', in plain ASCII form.

concepts.title: Expenditure Method: GDP from the Demand Side

questions.q: Compute GDP by the expenditure method from consumption investment government and net exports. Use the method 'Expenditure Method: GDP from the Demand Side'. Work with: consumption = 15, exports = 6, government_spending = 20, imports = 18, investment = 10. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of gdp_expenditure_method.

Find national output from C I G and the foreign trade balance. Use the method 'Expenditure Method: GDP from the Demand Side'. Work with: consumption = 30, exports = 8, government_spending = 500, imports = 4, investment = 300. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of gdp_expenditure_method.
Explain in your own words what 'Expenditure Method: GDP from the Demand Side' refers to.
questions.a: GDP can be totaled by adding all final spending on domestically produced goods - household consumption, firms' investment, government purchases and exports - and subtracting the import component embedded in each.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Expenditure Method: GDP from the Demand Side'.
questions.a: Only final expenditures enter, and imports are deducted because they are not produced domestically.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Expenditure Method: GDP from the Demand Side', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: gdp_expenditure_method = consumption + investment + government_spending + exports - imports

concepts.title: Income Method: GDP as Sum of Factor Incomes

questions.q: Find national output from the factor incomes of all households. Use the method 'Income Method: GDP as Sum of Factor Incomes'. Work with: gross_profits = 80000, interest_payments = 8, rents = 50, wages = 10. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of gdp_income_method.

Compute income-method GDP when wages are 80 and profits 120. Use the method 'Income Method: GDP as Sum of Factor Incomes'. Work with: gross_profits = 120000, interest_payments = 12, rents = 100, wages = 200. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of gdp_income_method.
Explain in your own words what 'Income Method: GDP as Sum of Factor Incomes' refers to.
questions.a: Since every firm's revenue ends up as payments to the factors it hires, GDP equals the total of wages, profits, interest and rent earned by all households in a year.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Income Method: GDP as Sum of Factor Incomes'.
questions.a: The distribution phase of the same circular flow adds up factor incomes to GDP.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Income Method: GDP as Sum of Factor Incomes', in plain ASCII form.

concepts.title: Factor Cost, Basic Prices and Market Prices

questions.q: Using the method 'Factor Cost, Basic Prices and Market Prices', work with: gva_factor_cost = 500, net_product_taxes = 25, net_production_taxes = 5. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of gdp_market_prices.

Take the relation taught for 'Factor Cost, Basic Prices and Market Prices' and work with: gva_factor_cost = 500, net_product_taxes = 8, net_production_taxes = 8. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of gdp_market_prices.
Explain in your own words what 'Factor Cost, Basic Prices and Market Prices' refers to.
questions.a: Factor cost keeps only payments to factors; adding production taxes net of production subsidies gives GVA at basic prices, and adding product taxes net of product subsidies on top raises it to market prices.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Factor Cost, Basic Prices and Market Prices'.
questions.a: Production taxes are fixed per producer while product taxes ride per unit of output; each net pair lifts the valuation one step.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Factor Cost, Basic Prices and Market Prices', in plain ASCII form.

concepts.title: GNP, NNP and National Income Chain

questions.q: Calculate GNP when GDP and net factor income from abroad are given. Use the method 'GNP, NNP and National Income Chain'. Work with: depreciation = 120000, gdp = 2500, indirect_taxes = 5, net_factor_income_from_abroad = 120000, subsidies = 400. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of national_income.

Find NNP at factor cost from NNP at market prices and net indirect taxes. Use the method 'GNP, NNP and National Income Chain'. Work with: depreciation = 120000, gdp = 8000, indirect_taxes = 20, net_factor_income_from_abroad = 120000, subsidies = 500. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of national_income.
Explain in your own words what 'GNP, NNP and National Income Chain' refers to.
questions.a: Adding net factor income from abroad to GDP gives GNP; deducting depreciation gives NNP at market prices; deducting net indirect taxes from that gives NNP at factor cost, which is national income.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'GNP, NNP and National Income Chain'.
questions.a: Each step removes one wedge: borders (NFIA), capital wear (depreciation) and government price wedges (net indirect taxes).

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'GNP, NNP and National Income Chain', in plain ASCII form.

concepts.title: Personal Income and Personal Disposable Income

questions.q: Compute personal disposable income after personal taxes and fines. Use the method 'Personal Income and Personal Disposable Income'. Work with: corporate_tax = 10, national_income = 1200, net_interest_paid_by_households = 20, non_tax_payments = 5, personal_taxes = 20, transfer_payments = 150, undistributed_profits = 500. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of personal_disposable_income.

Find the spendable income of households from national income data. Use the method 'Personal Income and Personal Disposable Income'. Work with: corporate_tax = 12, national_income = 2500, net_interest_paid_by_households = 18, non_tax_payments = 20, personal_taxes = 8, transfer_payments = 10, undistributed_profits = 12000. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of personal_disposable_income.
Explain in your own words what 'Personal Income and Personal Disposable Income' refers to.
questions.a: Personal income is the slice of national income actually reaching households, found by removing retained earnings, corporate tax and net interest paid by households while adding transfer receipts; disposable income is what remains after personal taxes and fines.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Personal Income and Personal Disposable Income'.
questions.a: Not all national income lands in household hands, and not all household income is freely spendable.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Personal Income and Personal Disposable Income', in plain ASCII form.

concepts.title: Nominal GDP, Real GDP and the GDP Deflator

questions.q: Calculate real GDP of the current year at base year prices. Use the method 'Nominal GDP, Real GDP and the GDP Deflator'. Work with: base_year_price = 2600, current_year_price = 2600, current_year_quantity = 50. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of gdp_deflator.

Find the GDP deflator from nominal and real GDP. Use the method 'Nominal GDP, Real GDP and the GDP Deflator'. Work with: base_year_price = 500, current_year_price = 2600, current_year_quantity = 1500. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of gdp_deflator.
Explain in your own words what 'Nominal GDP, Real GDP and the GDP Deflator' refers to.
questions.a: Nominal GDP values current output at current prices while real GDP values the same output at base-year prices; their ratio, the GDP deflator, isolates the pure price movement between the two years.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Nominal GDP, Real GDP and the GDP Deflator'.
questions.a: With quantities fixed at current levels, any gap between nominal and real GDP reflects prices alone.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Nominal GDP, Real GDP and the GDP Deflator', in plain ASCII form.

concepts.title: Consumer Price Index and Wholesale Price Index

questions.q: Compute the consumer price index from basket costs of two years. Use the method 'Consumer Price Index and Wholesale Price Index'. Work with: base_price_good1 = 8000, base_price_good2 = 120000, current_price_good1 = 80000, current_price_good2 = 20000, quantity_good1 = 45, quantity_good2 = 18. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of consumer_price_index.

Find the percentage rise in the cost of living between two years. Use the method 'Consumer Price Index and Wholesale Price Index'. Work with: base_price_good1 = 50000, base_price_good2 = 12000, current_price_good1 = 8000, current_price_good2 = 8000, quantity_good1 = 400, quantity_good2 = 15. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of consumer_price_index.
Explain in your own words what 'Consumer Price Index and Wholesale Price Index' refers to.
questions.a: The CPI prices a fixed basket bought by a typical consumer in the base year and again in the current year, then expresses the current cost as a percentage of the base cost; the WPI does the same for bulk-traded wholesale goods.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Consumer Price Index and Wholesale Price Index'.
questions.a: A fixed basket turns price change into a single index number.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Consumer Price Index and Wholesale Price Index', in plain ASCII form.

concepts.title: Limits of GDP as a Welfare Index

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Limits of GDP as a Welfare Index' refers to.
questions.a: Rising GDP need not mean rising wellbeing because its distribution may be skewed, unpaid non-monetary work and barter escape the accounts, and external harms or benefits carry no market price to correct the measure.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Limits of GDP as a Welfare Index'.
questions.a: Three gaps - uneven distribution, unpriced activity and externalities - keep GDP from tracking welfare closely.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Limits of GDP as a Welfare Index', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: welfare_gap = gdp_level - true_wellbeing (distribution, non-monetary exchanges, externalities)
